details:
**Moby-Dick and "Call me Ishmael"**
Melville's masterpiece (1851), an epic novel about a whaling voyage that opens with the famous line "Call me Ishmael." The narrator Ishmael is a wandering sailor who signs on to the whaling ship Pequod out of Nantucket and is the only one to survive its voyage.

**Captain Ahab and the white whale**
Ahab is the Pequod's monomaniacal one-legged captain, who lost his leg to the great white sperm whale Moby Dick and turns the voyage into a hunt for revenge. In the final three-day chase, he hurls his harpoon crying "From hell's heart I stab at thee," and he is dragged under by the line as the whale sinks the ship.

**Queequeg and his coffin**
Queequeg is a tattooed Polynesian harpooner whom Ishmael is forced to share a bed with at a crowded inn, and they become close friends. When Queequeg falls ill, he has a coffin built, which later becomes the ship's life buoy. Ishmael floats on it after the Pequod sinks until he is picked up by the Rachel, a ship searching for its captain's lost son.

**Starbuck, Fedallah, and the Pequod's crew**
Starbuck is the Pequod's sober Quaker first mate, who opposes Ahab's quest, and Stubb and Flask are the other mates. The harpooners are Queequeg, Tashtego, and the giant African Daggoo. Fedallah, a turbaned Parsee (Zoroastrian) whom Ahab secretly brings aboard, makes three prophecies about Ahab's death, including that only hemp can kill him. Before the voyage, the Quaker owners Bildad and Peleg sign Ishmael on, and Bildad's sister Aunt Charity brings Bibles and a copy of Watts.

**The gold doubloon**
Ahab nails a Spanish gold doubloon to the Pequod's mainmast as a reward for the first man to sight Moby Dick. Each crewman reads the coin's symbols differently, and Ahab ends up claiming it himself when he is the first to spot the whale.

**Pip, Father Mapple, and other Moby-Dick episodes**
Pip, the young Black cabin boy, goes mad after jumping overboard from a whaleboat and being left alone at sea. Before the voyage, Father Mapple preaches a sermon on Jonah from a pulpit shaped like a ship's prow. At sea, Tashtego falls into the spermaceti-filled "case" of a whale's head and is rescued, and the one-armed Captain Boomer of the Samuel Enderby cannot understand Ahab's thirst for revenge.

**"Bartleby, the Scrivener: A Story of Wall Street"**
Melville's most famous short story (1853). An unnamed Wall Street lawyer hires Bartleby, a pale copyist who soon answers every request with "I would prefer not to." He stops working entirely and refuses to leave the office, so the lawyer moves his offices away instead.

**Turkey, Nippers, Ginger Nut, and the Tombs**
The narrator's other employees in "Bartleby": the copyists Turkey and Nippers, who are each useful for only half the day, and the office boy Ginger Nut, named for the ginger cakes he fetches (the only food Bartleby seems to eat). Bartleby is taken to the Tombs prison, where he refuses to eat even though the lawyer pays a "grub-man" to feed him, and he dies there. The narrator later hears that Bartleby once worked in a Dead Letter Office, and the story ends "Ah Bartleby! Ah humanity!"

**"Benito Cereno"**
A novella about the American captain Amasa Delano, who boards the struggling Spanish slave ship San Dominick and fails to realize that the enslaved Africans, led by Babo, have revolted and are holding the nervous Spanish captain Benito Cereno hostage. In a tense scene, Babo shaves Cereno with a razor and draws blood. Babo is later executed, and his head, a "hive of subtlety," is set on a pole.

**"Follow your leader" and "what has cast such a shadow upon you?"**
In "Benito Cereno," the ship's figurehead is covered by canvas. When the canvas falls, it reveals the skeleton of the slaveowner Alexandro Aranda with the words "Follow your leader" chalked beneath it. Delano later asks the rescued Cereno, "You are saved; what has cast such a shadow upon you?" (Cereno answers "The negro"), and Ralph Ellison used the exchange as an epigraph for Invisible Man.

**Billy Budd, Sailor**
Melville's last novella, published after his death in 1924. Billy is a handsome, innocent "Handsome Sailor" impressed from the merchant ship Rights-of-Man onto the HMS Bellipotent. The envious master-at-arms John Claggart harasses him through the corporal Squeak and then falsely accuses him of mutiny. Billy, who stutters, cannot speak and strikes Claggart dead. Captain Vere has him hanged ("an angel of God! Yet the angel must hang!"), and Billy's last words are "God bless Captain Vere!" Vere later dies murmuring "Billy Budd."

**The Piazza Tales**
Melville's 1856 story collection containing "Bartleby" and "Benito Cereno." It also includes "The Lightning-Rod Man," in which a salesman fails to scare the narrator into buying a lightning rod during a thunderstorm; "The Bell-Tower," in which the architect Bannadonna is killed by his own automaton (the magistrates are unsettled that Una, one of the figures cast on the bell, looks unlike her sisters); and "The Encantadas," ten sketches of the Galápagos Islands, including the story of the stranded widow Hunilla.

**Typee**
Melville's first novel (1846), subtitled "A Peep at Polynesian Life" and based on his own experience. The narrator Tommo and his friend Toby jump ship from the whaler Dolly and live among the Typee people, rumored cannibals, in a valley of Nuku Hiva in the Marquesas Islands.

**Pierre, Israel Potter, and The Confidence-Man**
In Pierre; or, The Ambiguities, Pierre Glendinning breaks his engagement to Lucy Tartan to protect his illegitimate half-sister Isabel and later kills his cousin Glendinning Stanly. Israel Potter follows a Revolutionary War veteran who meets George III and becomes a spy for Benjamin Franklin. The Confidence-Man follows a shape-shifting swindler who deceives passengers on the Mississippi steamboat Fidèle on April Fools' Day.

**Melville's poetry and other writings**
His Civil War poetry collection Battle-Pieces opens with "The Portent," about the hanging of John Brown, and his late collection Timoleon is named for a poem about the ancient Corinthian statesman Timoleon. His sketch "The Paradise of Bachelors and the Tartarus of Maids" contrasts a London lawyers' dinner with a grim New England paper mill. His earliest work was "Fragments from a Writing Desk," and Hart Crane wrote the poem "At Melville's Tomb."
